summary: Describes using the Common Open Policy Service protocol to provision policy to network devices. This document is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: COPS-PR describes how a policy server can provision configuration to a network device. The device reports its capabilities, receives policy data, and reports whether it applied the changes.

questions: how does a policy server configure devices
what is a policy information base
how do network policies roll back on error
subtitle: A COPS usage for sending policy configuration from policy servers to network devices.

tldr.problem: Network devices need policy configuration such as quality-of-service settings, and providers need a protocol to communicate policy data to those devices.
tldr.mechanism: COPS-PR uses the COPS protocol to exchange policy provisioning data between a Policy Decision Point and Policy Enforcement Point, using named instances in a Policy Information Base.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3084 is Historic. It specifies how provisioning data is carried and applied, independent of the policy type or data model.

today: RFC 3084 is Historic and was published in March 2001. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document describes using COPS to carry policy-provisioning data.

sections.title: Policy Provisioning Model
sections.content:
COPS supports policy decisions between a Policy Decision Point (PDP) and a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP). This RFC describes the provisioning model, where the PDP can send configuration proactively rather than responding to each individual event at the PEP.

The protocol is independent of the kind of policy being provisioned. The examples focus on quality-of-service policy, but the message mechanisms carry policy data described in separate models.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDP is the policy server and a PEP is the device that applies policy. In provisioning, the server can send configuration changes without waiting for a separate request for each decision.

sections.title: Policy Information Base
sections.content:
Policy data is organized in a Policy Information Base (PIB), a conceptual tree of Provisioning Classes (PRCs) and their Provisioning Instances (PRIs). Each instance is identified by a Provisioning Instance Identifier (PRID) within its client type and request state.

The protocol supports installing or updating an instance and removing an instance or group identified by a prefix. The RFC also describes how PIBs may add or deprecate classes and attributes while allowing older and newer implementations to interoperate where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: A PIB organizes types of policy data and individual instances of those types. A PRID names an instance so the server can install, update, or remove it.

sections.title: Requests, Decisions, and Reports
sections.content:
The PEP opens a COPS connection and sends a configuration request describing its resources, supported policy information, and current state. This request asks for suitable policy data and opens a request state through which the PDP can send later updates.

The PDP sends decisions containing policy data to install or remove. The PEP returns a report indicating success or failure. If it rejects a decision, it rolls back to the previously installed good state. The PDP may send additional decisions asynchronously while the request state remains open.
sections.plainLanguage: The device reports what it supports and what policy it has installed. The server sends policy changes, and the device reports whether each change succeeded.

sections.title: Policy Data and Error Reports
sections.content:
COPS-PR carries named policy data in COPS client-specific objects. A PRID identifies the policy instance, and Encoded Provisioning Instance Data carries the instance values.

Error objects can report failures affecting the whole provisioning operation or a specific policy class. Reports can identify the rejected data so the PDP can adjust its decision and try again.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages identify the policy item and carry its values. If a device cannot apply the data, it can report an error and identify the problem for the server.

sections.title: Connection Loss and Security
sections.content:
If the TCP connection is lost, the PEP attempts to reconnect to its last PDP and can try a configured secondary PDP. The peers may synchronize state after reconnecting; while disconnected, the PEP continues using its active request state until the configured timeout behavior applies.

COPS supplies mandatory security mechanisms for authenticated and secure transfer. COPS-PR defines the structure of the carried policy data; documents defining particular PIBs must discuss security concerns specific to that data.
sections.plainLanguage: After a connection failure, the device can reconnect and synchronize policy state with a server. Security for the exchange comes from COPS, while each policy data model must address risks specific to its own fields.
